title: Why is every fraction in this odd number pattern one third?
description: Three fractions are made from sums of odd numbers, and each one equals one third. A letter for how many odd numbers are added shows that the bottom sum is always three times the top sum.
teaching_notes: One idea: use a letter for how many odd numbers the top sum has, and the rule that the first n odd numbers add up to n times n. Watch for students who say the bottom sum is two times the top, instead of taking away the top part.

video_script.why: The child uses a letter for a count we choose, as in the cycle puzzle, and the rule for the sum of odd numbers to explain a pattern in fractions.
video_script.substitution: Top sum of the first n odd numbers = n × n; the first 2n odd numbers add to 2n × 2n = 4 × n × n; bottom = 4 × n × n − n × n = 3 × n × n; fraction = 1 ÷ 3.
video_script.anchor: the three fractions in a row, with the top and bottom sums of odd numbers
video_script.payoff_line: Every fraction is one third, because the bottom sum is three times the top sum

final_answer.value: Every fraction equals one third, because the bottom sum is three times the top sum
final_answer.spoken: every fraction is one third, because the bottom sum is three times the top sum

video_script.fraction_reading: one third is read as one divided by three
maths_rules: the first n odd numbers add up to n × n
the first 2n odd numbers add up to 2n × 2n = 4 × n × n
bottom sum = 4 × n × n − n × n = 3 × n × n, three times the top sum n × n
video_script.design: One idea: a letter for how many odd numbers the top sum has, and the sum rule, show that the bottom sum is three times the top sum. The three fractions stay on the board and the check is the last step.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; the fractions 1 ÷ 3, (1 + 3) ÷ (5 + 7) and (1 + 3 + 5) ÷ (7 + 9 + 11) written in a row

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.ask: the words what do you notice? and why? appear

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book. Look at three fractions made from odd numbers.
<bookmark mark='first'/>The first is one divided by three.
<bookmark mark='second'/>The second is one plus three, divided by five plus seven.
<bookmark mark='third'/>The third is one plus three plus five, divided by seven plus nine plus eleven.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What do you notice, and can you explain why it happens?

beats.on_screen: the three fractions stay on the board while the child thinks

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the first n odd numbers add up to n × n; such as 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 = 3 × 3

marks.rule: the rule n × n is written
marks.three: the case 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 = 3 × 3 is written below it

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Recall that the first en odd numbers add up to en times en.
<bookmark mark='three'/>For three odd numbers, one plus three plus five is nine, which is three times three.

beats.on_screen: Given: three fractions made from sums of consecutive odd numbers

marks.given: the three fractions are shown again in a row

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, three fractions made from sums of odd numbers, taken one after another.

beats.on_screen: To find: what the fractions have in common, and why

marks.find: the words in common and why are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find what the fractions have in common, and why.
<bookmark mark='first'/>Step one, work out the first two fractions. One divided by three is one third.
<bookmark mark='sums'/>One plus three is four, and five plus seven is twelve.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Four divided by twelve is also one third.
<bookmark mark='top'/>Step two, the third fraction. One plus three plus five is nine.
<bookmark mark='bottom'/>Seven plus nine plus eleven is twenty seven.
<bookmark mark='third'/>Nine divided by twenty seven is again one third.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: top = the first n odd numbers = n × n; the first 2n odd numbers = 2n × 2n = 4 × n × n

marks.top: the top sum n × n is written
marks.twice: the first 2n odd numbers = 2n × 2n = 4 × n × n is written

beats.colours: top part and bottom part in two colours
narration: <bookmark mark='top'/>Step three, ask why. The top sum has the first en odd numbers, so it is en times en.
<bookmark mark='twice'/>The first two en odd numbers add up to two en times two en. That is four times en times en.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: bottom = 4 × n × n − n × n = 3 × n × n; fraction = (n × n) ÷ (3 × n × n)

marks.left: n × n is taken away from 4 × n × n
marks.bottom: 3 × n × n is written as the bottom sum
marks.frac: (n × n) ÷ (3 × n × n) is written and the common part is cancelled

narration: <bookmark mark='left'/>Step four, the bottom sum is what is left after taking away the top part.
<bookmark mark='bottom'/>Four times en times en take away en times en leaves three times en times en.
<bookmark mark='frac'/>The bottom sum is three times the top sum, so the fraction is one divided by three.

beats.on_screen: Step 5, check with n = 3: top = 9, bottom = 3 × 9 = 27, 9 ÷ 27

marks.bottom: the bottom 3 × 9 = 27 is written and ticked

narration: <bookmark mark='top'/>Step five, check with en equal to three. The top is nine.
<bookmark mark='bottom'/>The bottom is three times nine, which is twenty seven, the same as the third fraction.

beats.on_screen: Answer: Every fraction is one third, because the bottom sum is three times the top sum
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Every fraction is one third, because the bottom sum is three times the top sum.
